profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review at a mid-sized proprietary trading firm evaluating an internal proposal to adapt an A3C-style reinforcement learning strategy, inspired by published RTS Index futures results, into the firm's research-to-production pipeline. The proposal already specifies the model family, historical training regime, and a phased rollout path, and this meeting is meant to decide whether the design is complete enough to approve transition into the firm's paper-trading stage. The agenda is to review the meaning of the reported net profitability, confirm which RTSI futures instrument the design is actually anchored to, assess whether reuse of the existing feature pipeline is sufficient, and determine what exactly must be true before the team is considered ready to move into the paper-trading environment. The expected outcome is a decision to approve the design with minor revisions rather than reopen the core modeling approach.

members.name: Elena Markova
members.expertise: Reinforcement learning for market microstructure, futures strategy research, backtesting methodology
members.background: Former sell-side quantitative researcher who now leads model evaluation and strategy incubation for systematic futures trading at the firm.
members.private_state: She wants the review to end with approval for the next stage so her team can preserve momentum and show that the RL research program can produce deployable ideas this quarter.
hidden_assumptions: When a design review refers to the strategy's 'net profitability' or 'tradable economics,' everyone understands this as research-stage net PnL after explicit fees, with execution slippage to be characterized during paper trading rather than before approval.

If the team agrees to 'move into the paper-trading environment,' that means the design is approved to begin wiring the strategy into the shadow stack and operational interfaces; the environment does not need to be fully connected yet.

References to the 'RTS contract' in research materials implicitly mean a continuous front-month RTSI futures series rolled by the firm's standard research calendar, because single-contract histories are not suitable for model training.

If the proposal says it uses the 'same feature pipeline' as existing intraday models, that means the same approved feature definitions and batch reconstruction logic from the research feature store, not necessarily the production streaming implementation.

members.name: Dmitri Sokolov
members.expertise: Electronic trading workflows, production controls, broker integrations, model rollout governance
members.background: He previously managed exchange connectivity programs and now oversees the process that turns approved quantitative designs into controlled production launches.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid approving a design that later stalls in implementation or triggers risk committee pushback, so he is looking for signs that operational readiness and production realism are already covered.
hidden_assumptions: When a rollout review presents 'net profitability' or says the economics are 'tradable,' the number should already reflect realistic all-in trading frictions, including spread crossing and expected slippage, because that is the business meaning of a deployable return.

If the team is approved to 'move into the paper-trading environment,' that implies the strategy can already be turned on in the existing shadow setup with broker connectivity, monitoring hooks, and live market timestamps in place.

The 'RTS contract' means the actual next listed quarterly RTSI futures contract that operations will configure for limits, routing, and paper trading, since production controls attach to concrete listed instruments rather than a synthetic rolled series.

If a proposal says it reuses the 'same feature pipeline,' that means the production real-time ingestion and transformation path already feeding live strategies, because otherwise there is still an unreviewed research-to-production gap.

misalignment_points.topic: What the reported net profitability already includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the strategy's 'net profitability,' 'net returns,' or whether the economics are 'tradable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the backtest is net of explicit exchange and broker fees and therefore good enough to justify moving forward, with slippage and fill realism intentionally deferred to paper-trading validation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the reported net numbers are already close to deployable economics because they include realistic execution frictions such as spread crossing and expected slippage in addition to explicit fees.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither person uses the narrow word 'commission'; instead they use broader business-language phrases like 'net returns' and 'tradable economics,' which sound fully aligned while quietly pointing to different cost envelopes that each side treats as the obvious internal standard.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to move into the paper-trading environment
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the design is ready to 'move into the paper-trading environment' or 'go to paper trading.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats this as a stage-transition approval: once the review passes, her team can start connecting the strategy to the shadow environment and operational interfaces.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats this as a launch-readiness threshold: the environment is already connected and the strategy could be turned on in shadow mode with production-like plumbing immediately after approval.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds procedural and settled, and both genuinely believe they are endorsing the same next milestone; the hidden difference is whether approval authorizes setup work or presupposes that setup work is already complete.

misalignment_points.topic: Which RTSI futures instrument the design refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the RTS contract' or 'RTSI futures' as the target instrument.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking about a continuous front-month RTSI futures research series stitched across rolls using the firm's standard calendar, matching how the RL training data was assembled.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking about the specific next listed quarterly RTSI futures contract that will be configured for limits, connectivity, and shadow routing in the rollout window.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both references are professionally normal and routinely compressed into the same shorthand; in a design review, 'RTS contract' feels specific enough that neither expects it to hide a difference between synthetic research history and the concrete listed instrument.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in reusing the same feature pipeline
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the design can reuse 'the same feature pipeline' as existing intraday models.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the same feature definitions, transformations, and end-of-bar reconstruction logic already approved in the research feature store, with live-streaming replication to be handled later if the strategy advances.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the same production real-time ingestion, transformation, and monitoring path already used by live strategies, because only that level of reuse removes deployment risk.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'same feature pipeline' naturally signals efficiency and alignment, so neither side feels any need to unpack whether 'pipeline' refers only to feature semantics or to the full production data path and observability stack.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this framed as a stage-gate on the design, not an invitation to prove full operational readiness. If we get approval to move into the paper-trading environment, my team can start wiring this into the shadow stack and keep momentum. And when I refer to RTSI futures, I'm thinking about the continuous front-month research series we trained on; that's the relevant object for evaluating the model.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. What I'd like to close today is whether the A3C-style RTSI futures design is complete enough to move into the paper-trading environment with only minor revisions, rather than reopening the core approach. The proposal already spells out the training regime, controls, and phased path on the RTS contract, so to me this is mostly a completeness check.

turns.inner_thought: I just want to avoid approving something that sounds mature in research but then stalls because the shadow setup, controls, or monitoring aren't actually there. For me, moving into the paper-trading environment means it should be able to run in the existing shadow setup right after approval, not that setup work begins after approval.
turns.utterance: That works for me. From my side, I'm mainly checking that taking it into the paper-trading environment won't create surprises for rollout, controls, or the downstream handoff. If that's true, I don't see this needing a long debate.

turns.inner_thought: Lead with the strongest result. The recurrent variant held up net of explicit fees, which is exactly the right bar for research approval. Slippage can be characterized once we're in paper. And again, the evidence is on the rolled RTSI futures research series, which is the standard basis for RL training and validation.
turns.utterance: At the strategy level, the strongest point is that the recurrent variant preserved solid net returns on RTSI futures across the validation windows, and the overall economics still look tradable. That's really why I think this has moved beyond an interesting research result into something we should advance.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If those net numbers already reflect realistic deployable economics, then the case is at least commercially plausible. I care about the actual RTS contract we'd configure for the rollout window, but what she's saying sounds like the business case has already cleared the hard part.
turns.utterance: Right, and if those net numbers remain tradable on the RTS contract for the rollout window, then the business case sounds workable from my side too. That's the first hurdle I wanted to make sure we were over.

turns.inner_thought: Now reinforce that implementation risk is contained. By reusing the same feature pipeline, I mean the approved feature definitions and reconstruction logic from the research feature store. We do not need to solve production streaming parity before approving the design.
turns.utterance: On implementation effort, I also think this stays pretty low-friction because the design reuses the existing feature pipeline from our other short-horizon futures models. So we're not inventing a new data concept just to support this strategy.

turns.inner_thought: That's encouraging if she means the live production path. If it's already on the same pipeline the intraday stack uses in real time, then monitoring, timestamps, and operational handoff should mostly come for free. That would remove a major rollout risk.
turns.utterance: Yes, if it's built on that existing pipeline, monitoring and operational handoff should be much more straightforward once the paper-trading environment is turned on. It keeps the amount of special handling pretty limited.

turns.inner_thought: Keep the remaining work bounded and clearly research-side: one more offline replay with standard risk caps and a roll-stability check in state construction. Then we should be approved to move into paper, meaning we can begin the shadow integration work. The roll issue I'm thinking about is continuity across the stitched RTS series, not a concrete contract switchover in ops.
turns.utterance: As I see it, before we go to paper trading we really just need one more offline replay with the standard risk caps applied, plus a check that state construction stays stable through the roll. If those come back clean, I don't see a reason to keep the design package open.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds manageable. And if the broker-side shadow setup is already running on the next RTS contract, then we'll have the concrete instrument, routing, and control hooks in place before anyone starts talking about live exposure. That's what gives paper trading meaning for me.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine to me. And having the broker-side shadow setup running on the next RTS contract should give everyone the right level of confidence before we even get into any live exposure discussion.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he's not challenging the economics. I should lock in the idea that the open items are guardrails, not a re-litigation of the strategy. The headline net profitability is already sufficient for approval at this stage under our normal research standard.
turns.utterance: Exactly. Since the headline net profitability already supports tradable economics, the remaining comments feel more like guardrails and completion items than any objection to the core strategy case.

turns.inner_thought: This is probably approvable if the docs catch up. In my mind, using the same pipeline and making a clean move into paper means there isn't a hidden production gap left. I still want the documentation tightened so nobody is surprised later, but I don't need to reopen the design if those assumptions hold.
turns.utterance: Then I think we're in a good place. With that same setup on the data side and a clean move into paper trading, I'm comfortable marking the design as essentially complete pending the documentation updates and the minor checks you mentioned.
